facts.title: Mi Jin Kim’s short stories explore the ambiguities of human connection
facts.description: Every semester, at least one student asks me why I love books. Without skipping a beat, I reply that books are links between human beings. Centuries ago, someone went through the same thing you did. They wrote about their experience, and that book connects us to them. Through books, we are never truly alone. Mi Jin Kim’s Invitations is one of those books, focusing on the connections between people and what those relationships change within us. Through a series of short stories, the reader follows multiple characters as they attempt to navigate connections – and missed connections – in their own lives. The short stories in Invitations include characters of diverse ages who find themselves in a variety of situations. From a newly-divorced older man to a woman going to the wedding of a childhood friend, to estranged brothers reconnecting from two different continents, the characters aren’t particularly extraordinary. In fact, I would go as far as to say they are the opposite: they are extremely ordinary and familiar. The relatability of a character is usually a cliché, one easily avoided by more in-depth reading, but in the case of Kim’s stories, the relatable moments and reactions of the characters kept me reading. Two prominent Northwest figures are currently memorialized and celebrated in the Cascadia Art Museum: Shiro Miyazaki’s “Light of Remembrance,” and Zoe Dusanne’s “The Art of Seeing,” are both on display until January 3rd, 2027. Shiro Miyazaki: “Light of Remembrance”. Shiro Miyazaki’s exhibit features his extensive body of art that he created during his short and turbulent life. His linocuts and watercolor pieces depict landscapes, stills, and portraits that often convey political commentary or a sort of social message contextualized by the heightened unrest in Japan and the US. Miyazaki (1910–1940), born in Nara Prefecture in Japan, grew up in poverty and, while working as a nomadic farm laborer, used the fruits and vegetables he harvested as painting subjects and then as his meal once he was finished. As recognition for his art grew, his health unfortunately deteriorated and he died of advanced-stage lung cancer at the age of thirty. Throughout the exhibit, many emotions surround Miyazaki’s pieces. One of these pieces, For the Fruits of Our Labor, is a linocut on red paper, circa 1938. Depicting a hand reaching for fruit, the image might be interpreted as a blending of his time as a farm laborer, his tumultuous life, and his declining health manifested in a hand tied down by what looks like smoke, just out of reach of the fruit and light of the sun. facts.description: Left: A poster for “Nanay.” Right: playwright Molly Olis Krost. Courtesy image. Two long-standing performing arts organizations, Pork Filled Productions and Theatre Off Jackson, are partnering this autumn to present a world premiere by playwright Molly Olis Krost. Directed by Alyza DelPan-Monley, Krost’s play Nanay centers on adult twin sisters Eve and Angela as they struggle to reconnect following the birth of Eve’s new baby. Throughout the play, Eve and Angela explore their Filipino cultural history and traditions while remembering their nanay, a Tagalog word for mother, who is often viewed as a source of unconditional love as well as the emotional anchor of the family. At the same time, Angela cautiously approaches Eve’s domestic companion Ernesto, who happens to be a Manananggal, a demon that is one variety of many malevolent, shape-shifting creatures in Filipino mythology known as the aswang. By day, Ernesto appears as a typical human, while at night, he transforms into a monster whose hunger is for the hearts and livers of children or unborn fetuses. facts.description: Illustration by Ryan Catabay/DRGDRP Creative. The new Bruce Lee Way sits on the south side of Hing Hay, between Sixth Avenue South and Maynard Avenue South, in the neighborhood where a young Lee made his mark. That Friday morning ceremony drew scores of community members and city officials to celebrate the street renaming. Many attendees wore Bruce Lee merch. One person dressed up in Lee’s iconic yellow jumpsuit from his unfinished film “Game of Death.”. “Today, Seattle is recognizing an important part of Bruce Lee’s extraordinary journey from a young martial arts instructor in Seattle, to international icon,” said Abe Santos, co-founder of Jun Fan Gung Fu Academy and advocate for the sign. “His influence continues to inspire generations, and now his name will forever be part of the city that helped shape him.”. facts.title: New Mount Zion Pastor Rev. Johnson Shares Vision Ahead Of Installation Weekend
facts.description: Rev. Charles Reginald Johnson Sr. joins the Seattle Medium's Rhythm & News Podcast to discuss his new role as senior pastor of Mount Zion Baptist Church, a 135-year cornerstone of Seattle's Black community. After 17 years leading Cochran Avenue Baptist Church in Los Angeles, Johnson shares his vision ahead of his November 14-15 installation celebration.

facts.description: Marking its 36th year, the Judge Charles V. Johnson Youth and Law Forum returns Saturday, Nov. 14 in Tukwila, connecting young people and families with judges, attorneys and law enforcement. title: Lincoln Stuns Franklin 24-20 In Regular Season Finale

facts.title: Lincoln Stuns Franklin 24-20 In Regular Season Finale
facts.description: Lincoln ended a winless season with a stunning 24-20 upset over homecoming host Franklin, capped by quarterback Ben Ward's 61-yard touchdown pass to Zachary Nelson with 2:25 left. The Lynx defense then sealed the win with a goal-line stand, stopping Franklin's final drive on fourth down to secure their first victory.

facts.description: I didn’t understand Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget cuts to the fire department until I found myself giving CPR to a dying man in Magnolia, the kind of peripheral neighborhood of Seattle that is most at risk from her call to cut firefighter hours. It was 5:32 p.m. on that September afternoon when I heard someone collapse onto the dusty trail in Discovery Park, and saw a doctor giving a man CPR while a friend called 911. The question in that moment—When the fuck are the EMTs gonna get here?—is at the heart of the fight over the city budget that will be playing out in Seattle for at least the next few weeks. Wilson’s budget proposes cuts from all city departments, but identifies the biggest cut in the fire department, in the form of a $7 million cut to overtime. It’s part of Wilson’s effort to shrink spending and abandon budget tricks of her predecessors that achieved a legally required “balanced budget” by creating future debts. facts.title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns
facts.description: King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) CEO Dr. Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation today after only two years on the job. The announcement comes as the beleaguered agency is in the process of being partially dismantled. In a press release, the KCRHA governing board said Kinnison’s departure reflects the organization’s changes in “mission, purpose, and service scope.” Her resignation will be effective November 16. While Kinnison was not officially pushed out, her resignation is the latest in the ongoing fallout over the KCRHA’s damning forensic evaluation in April that found the agency had lost track of $13 million due to poor internal accounting practices. In response to the audit, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay decided in July to take back administration of about $160 million in homelessness service provider contracts, slashing the KCRHA’s budget by more than two thirds. That remnant was left in charge of coordinating the region’s $67 million grant application to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). It also keeps several regional functions, such as holding the biennial Point-in-Time census of homelessness in the county. The downscaling has already resulted in 10 layoffs, one voluntary departure and the elimination of six unfilled positions from the agency, PubliCola reported in August. title: Say Cheese!

facts.title: Say Cheese!
facts.description: There is something about this piece of cheese—waterslide transfer print on processed prepared cheese product, to be exact—that’s really doing it for me. Made by Texas-raised, Portland-based artist Ash Stone, it’s on view tonight at RailSpur as part of an exhibition called I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance. The image has been transferred onto the protective plastic sleeve sheathing a glisteny slice of orange cheese: a picture of a trailer, the kind of single- or double-wide you find plentiful in rural Texas. Surrounded by clusters of bright daylilies, an attached staircase-cum-porch leads to the closed front door, where a white-haired woman pauses, her body half-turned toward the viewer. The Mary in Mary’s Garden is Stone’s grandmother, and the raised flowerbeds in the foreground are hers. Another piece of cheese in the show, titled Some Day, is imprinted with words that seem to have been scrawled on a Post-it-sized note: “I love you and am SO proud of you. I’m sorry it’s not the way I had hoped here—maybe it will be some day.”. Ash Stone’s Some Day at RailSpur. Stone’s playfulness is as abundant as the faux cheese on the bottom shelf of a dairy display, and it operates on the same frequency as a Proustian madeleine. The words “say cheese” cling like an aura to the images, forcing smiles. title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto

facts.title: Councilmember Rob Saka Backs Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto
facts.description: At a press conference on Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson explained why she issued her first veto against the council’s recently passed RV ban and presented her own alternative executive order. But it was a surprise guest who stole the show: centrist City Councilmember Rob Saka. Saka’s presence signaled his reversal on the controversial RV bill, which he had voted for last month. Together with the three progressives on the council, Saka’s support will be enough to safeguard Wilson’s veto from a potential override. The legislation, sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss, would have required RV owners to obtain a special new permit to park their vehicles on city streets for more than two hours. But homelessness advocates and services providers argued the true intent of legislation was to “regulate” (read: banish) RV residents out of city limits altogether. Wilson echoed the concerns over the well-being of homeless vehicle residents, and also said that Strauss’s bill would expose the City to potential lawsuits. It would also cost millions of dollars to set up a new permitting bureaucracy, she said. “It is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said.
